title: Drop 1
summary: A small, real-world product drop to test demand, sourcing, positioning, and fulfilment without overbuilding.
why:
The fastest way to learn whether SIndustries can generate revenue is to actually try to generate revenue. Research and planning have diminishing returns without real market feedback.

A constrained commerce experiment forces decisions about sourcing, pricing, positioning, and fulfilment that can't be answered theoretically. Each step either works or produces evidence about why it doesn't.

Drop 1 is designed to be small enough to complete without significant capital commitment, but real enough that the outcomes are meaningful. The goal is a complete loop, not a polished result.
successCriteria:
A complete product drop runs end to end: sourcing a product, setting a price, publishing an offer, fulfilling at least one order, and capturing clear data on demand, margin, effort, and customer response.

Success is not revenue — it's evidence. Even a failed drop that surfaces clear data about what doesn't work is a successful experiment.

Key questions to answer: Can I source something viable in under a week? Does the positioning earn attention? What does fulfilment actually cost in time and money? Would I do it again at larger scale?
currentLearning: Sourcing research underway — evaluating 3 product candidates against margin, lead time, and SIndustries narrative fit.
Positioning hypothesis: the SIndustries audience responds to practical tools and systems, not lifestyle products.
Fulfilment approach TBD: exploring direct-to-consumer vs marketplace to understand control/effort tradeoff.

title: Social content
summary: Short-form public signal to build distribution, sharpen narrative, and learn what people respond to.
why:
Distribution is a structural problem. Without an audience or a reliable channel, every other experiment runs in a vacuum. Getting early signal about what earns attention is more valuable than optimising content quality in isolation.

X/Twitter is the first channel because the audience overlap with builders, founders, and technical practitioners is highest. The format — short-form threads and notes — is low-friction to produce and easy to iterate.

The goal isn't growth for its own sake. It's to understand which topics, formats, and claims earn useful engagement from people who might eventually become customers, collaborators, or advocates.
successCriteria:
A repeatable posting cadence is established and maintained for at least 30 days. Each piece of content generates observable signal: impressions, replies, follows, or link clicks.

By the end of the first cycle, I should be able to answer: What topics generate the most engagement from the right audience? What formats work best (threads vs. single posts vs. images)? What claims or framings earn the strongest reactions?

The secondary outcome is narrative sharpening — publishing forces clarity that internal thinking doesn't.

Cadence target revised in light of the content factory: the website ships a structured weekly update on a reliable cycle. Social posting should treat each weekly drop as source material for short-form distribution, not compete with it. Target: 1-2 social posts per week sourced from the weekly website update, plus standalone experiments when something warrants immediate signal.
currentLearning: Initial posts about OpenClaw and AI operations earned higher engagement than general SIndustries positioning content.
Build-in-public framing (showing the process, not just the result) consistently outperforms polished announcement-style posts.

The content factory changes the channel plan: weekly website updates are now a reliable source of short-form social material. Treating the website as the source of truth and social as the distribution layer removes the manual writing bottleneck that kept cadence at 1-2 posts per week.
Original cadence target (3-4 standalone posts per week) is being replaced by 1-2 distribution posts per week sourced from the weekly update. Quality and reliability matter more than raw post count.

2026-06-17 X thread on the Lobster + Quinn state-handoff pattern shifted the channel from announcement-style posts to architecture-and-process posts. The thread landed because it explains a real design decision (where intelligence lives in an agent pipeline) rather than selling a product outcome — supporting the hypothesis that process posts are now the strongest format for the SIndustries audience, not just a planned pivot.

title: Product Market Scans
summary: Recurring scans for gaps, pricing windows, underserved niches, and first-drop candidates.
why:
Inspiration is not a reliable source of product ideas. Systematic scanning is.

Most founder-led companies find their first products through personal pain or accidental discovery. Both are real signals, but they're biased toward the founder's specific context and they arrive randomly. A recurring scan process surfaces opportunities outside the founder's blind spots and creates a documented decision trail.

For SIndustries, the scan criteria are: Does it fit the systems/automation/builder narrative? Is there visible demand evidence? Can it be executed as a small team or solo? Is there a clear path from experiment to revenue?
successCriteria:
Scans run at least twice per month and produce a prioritised list of candidates with supporting evidence for each.

Each candidate record captures: the gap or opportunity, the evidence base, the key constraints, the effort estimate, and a go/no-go recommendation with reasoning.

Over time the scan database becomes a live list of tested hypotheses — things we looked at and rejected (with reasons), things we're actively pursuing, and things worth revisiting as conditions change.
currentLearning: First scan completed: identified 6 candidates across commerce, tools, and content. 2 advanced to further evaluation.
NZ-specific opportunities appear underexplored in the AI-native tools category — global tools often miss local compliance and context.
Recurring scans need a lightweight template to avoid inconsistent depth between cycles.

title: Plano model routing
summary: Local model routing for cheaper, faster, more autonomous agent work across routine operations.
why:
As agent workflows scale, the cost and latency of routing everything through frontier models becomes a real constraint. Not every task needs Claude Opus or GPT-4. Most routine operations — summarisation, classification, formatting, simple transformations — are well within the capability of smaller, faster, cheaper models.

Plano is an experiment in building the routing layer: classifying tasks by complexity and routing them to appropriate models. The hypothesis is that 60-70% of routine agent work can be offloaded to local or cheaper models with acceptable quality degradation, reducing cost by a significant margin.

The secondary benefit is latency: local models have sub-second response times for many tasks, which matters for interactive operations.
successCriteria:
A routing layer is operational that classifies incoming tasks and routes them to appropriate models. At least 50% of routine operations run through non-frontier models.

Quality benchmarks are established for key task types so routing decisions are evidence-based, not arbitrary. The system degrades gracefully — unclear cases escalate to frontier models rather than producing bad outputs silently.

Cost metrics are tracked before and after routing implementation to quantify the actual saving.
currentLearning: Initial routing prototype showed promising results for summarisation and classification tasks with llama3 variants.
Boundary conditions are harder than expected: tasks that seem simple often require judgment that smaller models handle poorly.
Routing by task type (summarise, classify, generate) works better than routing by estimated complexity.

Experiment killed 2026-07-03. The routing layer added complexity without sufficient quality/cost benefit at current workload scale. Frontier model costs are manageable; the overhead of maintaining routing logic and quality benchmarks outweighed the savings. Revisit if agent volume grows significantly.

title: NZ Personal Banking App
summary: A live-data mobile budgeting MVP for NZ households, wired to bank sync, balances, alerts, transaction views, spending breakdowns, and recategorisation.
why:
Most personal finance apps are built for a US context and don't fit NZ banking realities: open banking access, bank-specific quirks, and the specific spending patterns of NZ households.

The pain is real and personal. Tracking family net worth in Google Sheets for 2 hours a month is a solved problem waiting for better tooling. The interesting question isn't 'can an app do this' — they can — it's whether there's a viable wedge in the NZ market specifically.

If open banking APIs improve in NZ (the regulatory environment is moving in that direction), the data access problem becomes solvable. The UI/UX problem remains: most apps optimise for transaction history, not for the decision-support layer households actually need.
successCriteria:
The concept is sufficiently narrowed to identify: the specific user problem with evidence it's real and recurring, a credible data-access path given NZ banking constraints, and a prototype scope small enough to test with real users.

This is a go/no-go gate, not a build commitment. The outcome could be 'the constraint is access to bank data and the regulatory timeline makes this unviable right now' — that's a valid result.
currentLearning: The first end-to-end mobile build is now wired to live Akahu-backed bank data instead of mock screens.
Accounts, cards, balances, balance alerts, spending breakdowns, category transaction views, recategorisation, and transaction detail sheets are functional in the MVP.
The experiment has moved from market concept to product learning: the next useful evidence is whether the live-data flows make household decisions clearer in repeated use.

title: Roadmapping Scenarios App
summary: A scenario-driven planning surface for comparing paths, trade-offs, and sequencing decisions.
why:
Strategic planning is hard to do well in text or spreadsheets. The limitation isn't data — it's the inability to compare scenarios side by side with their downstream implications.

This idea comes from a specific frustration: trying to plan product roadmaps with multiple possible paths and needing to compare them on multiple dimensions simultaneously (effort, risk, revenue impact, dependencies). Existing tools are either too heavy (Gantt charts, JIRA) or too lightweight (sticky notes, docs).

The hypothesis is that a purpose-built scenario comparison surface — optimised for the decision moment, not for project tracking — would be valuable for technical leaders who make these calls regularly.
successCriteria:
A prototype helps compare at least two meaningful strategic paths with their constraints, trade-offs, and sequencing implications visible simultaneously.

The key usability test: does using the tool actually change the decision, or does it just visualise what was already obvious? If it surfaces non-obvious trade-offs, it has value.
